activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a series circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out.
story:
Nicolas pressed his badge against the glowing door of the museum's Tinkering Lab and practically bounced inside. Today was circuit day, and he had been counting down since Monday. At the workbench, Leonard was already dumping a pile of wire onto the table, and Mr. Shevchenko, the lab's keeper, slid a small tray toward them with a battery, a switch, two bulbs in holders, and a screwdriver.

"Your challenge," said Mr. Shevchenko, "is to make both bulbs light, then explain why they light." He pointed to a wall of paper boats floating in a water tank behind them. "And if you finish early, you can convert one of those sailboats into a paddle boat with rubber bands." Nicolas grinned. He loved that buoyant little fleet, every boat bobbing like it couldn't wait to be upgraded.

They clipped the wires, screwed the holders down, and flipped the switch. Both bulbs glowed. Leonard cheered, and even the kids at the next bench looked over. "See, the current goes out of the battery, through the switch, through this bulb, through that bulb, and back to the battery," Nicolas said, tracing the loop with his finger. "It's one circle. Mr. Shevchenko called it a series circuit." Then he had an idea. What if one bulb failed? Would the other one stay on? He unscrewed the first bulb just enough to break its connection, and both bulbs went dark at once. "Whoa," Leonard whispered. "They both died." Nicolas screwed it back in, flipped the switch, and both glowed again.

"So one broken bulb kills the whole loop," Nicolas said, jabbing the table. "Every bulb in the circuit goes out, not just the broken one." Mr. Shevchenko, passing by with an armload of wire, said nothing at all, which Nicolas took as the highest possible praise. He grabbed a rubber band and a cork and marched toward the water tank. "Okay," he called to Leonard, "now we make the fastest paddle boat this museum has ever seen."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: On eye prescriptions, OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye, from the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister.
story:
Hudson stood outside the eyeglass store at the mall with his exam paper folded in his back pocket, and next to him Pierce was reading over his shoulder anyway, because that was what Pierce did.

"Okay, so it says your prescription is OD minus one point five, OS minus one," Pierce said, squinting at the paper. "OD. Like, overdose? Hudson, what if something's wrong with your eyeballs and they wrote a code about it?"

"That's not a medical code," Hudson said, though his stomach did a small flip anyway. He looked at the paper again. The letters were printed in tiny capitals next to two numbers that were almost the same but not quite, and something about that bothered him. If OD and OS were warning codes, they wouldn't need two of them, one for each line. Two labels, two eyes. He turned the idea over. "Wait here."

He walked to the wall where the store kept a big printed chart about eye care for customers, because stores like this explained things to grown-ups all the time. He ran his finger down the column. There it was, in plain black print, and he read it twice to be sure.

"Pierce," he called, waving him over. "It says here OD means the right eye and OS means the left eye. From the Latin oculus dexter and oculus sinister." He pointed at each abbreviation as he said it. "So my right eye is a little worse than my left. No secret code."

Pierce exhaled so hard he fogged the display case. "Oculus sinister. That just sounds like a villain."

"Latin does that," said the optician behind the counter, grinning, and pulled a tray of frames toward them. "Pick a color, tough guy."

Choosing took forever. Hudson tried on a red pair that compressed uncomfortably against his temples until the optician bent the arms wider, and a silver pair that slid down his nose every time he looked at the floor. The third pair, dark blue with thin wire rims, sat still when he shook his head, and the mirror showed a kid who looked like himself, only more awake.

When the glasses were ready an hour later, Hudson slid them on in the middle of the food court. The world sharpened all at once. The menu board across the aisle, which had been a smudge of glowing color, now had distinct letters he could read from twenty feet away. Every scruffy letter of the pretzel stand sign stood apart from its neighbor, crisp as cut paper. He could see a single sesame seed on the floor near the trash cans.

"Read that," Pierce said, pointing at the far mall directory.

Hudson read it, all of it, down to the tiny store numbers. Then he took the prescription paper out, held it at arm's length, and read it too, out loud, both lines, right eye first.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
Laurence pushed the shopping cart past the cereal aisle, hunting for the shortest checkout line. Tonight was her turn to cook, and in the basket sat chicken thighs, lemons, rice, and a bottle of oil. She had written a letter to her mom that morning and left it on the fridge: "Dear Mom, I am making dinner tonight so you can rest. I watched you fry chicken last month and I will do the same thing. Love, Laurence." The words felt like a promise, and she intended to keep it.

At home, she heated the oil in the pan exactly as her mother had, waiting for it to shimmer. Her little brother wandered in to watch. The oil popped once, then flared, a ring of orange flame leaping up around the chicken. Laurence's hand flew toward the tap, and the glass by the sink was already full of water.

Then she stopped herself. She remembered the night her mother hadn't reached for water at all. The pan had flared the same way, and her mother had simply turned off the burner and slid a lid over the pan, and the flames had died as if the fire were a creature that had crawled somewhere to hibernate and never woke. Laurence had asked about it afterward, and Ms. Jung, her science teacher, had confirmed it later in class: "Water on a grease fire is the equivalent of throwing gasoline on it," Ms. Jung had said, which had made the whole class sit up straight. It was a phenomenon Laurence had turned over in her mind ever since.

Now she turned off the burner, grabbed the lid, and slid it over the pan. The flames shrank, flickered, and vanished. Her brother applauded with a wooden spoon. When their mother came home, she read the letter on the fridge, then followed the smell of lemon chicken into the kitchen and stopped in the doorway.

"You put the lid on," her mother said slowly. "Where did you learn that?"

"You," said Laurence. "Last month. You never once reached for water."

Her mother smiled and held up the letter. "So who wrote this? Your handwriting looks like mine."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood.
story:
Gabriella sat in the tall chair at the eyeglass counter and watched the optometrist slide a card across the counter. It said she was nearsighted in both eyes. "You'll want glasses for the board at school," he said, "and for movies. Interesting thing, though. Studies show that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors during childhood." He tapped the card once and went to check on another customer.

Gabriella thought about that while a saleswoman measured the distance between her pupils. She thought about it while she tried on purple frames, then silver ones. She thought about her own weekends, which she mostly spent on the couch with her tablet until she felt so lethargic she didn't want to move even to get a snack. Mikaela and Ariyah found her at the mirror, arms full of shopping bags.

"You're getting glasses?" Mikaela said. "Awesome. I want some but I don't need them."

"Come here," Gabriella said. "Question. When you were little, how much time did you spend outside?"

Ariyah shrugged. "Every day. My mom kicked us out of the house till dinner."

"Me too," Mikaela said. "Soccer, bikes, whatever."

Gabriella wrote their names in her notebook. Under them she wrote outdoor childhood, no glasses. Under her own name she wrote indoor weekends, nearsighted. Then she went to find her mother by the fountain.

"Can I ask the man one more thing?" she said. She walked back to the counter with the notebook open. "Hi. I have a question about what you said, that nearsightedness is less common in people who spent more time outdoors as kids. Does that mean it works the other way too? If I go outside a lot now, could it help?"

"It can't undo what you already have," the optometrist said. "You'll still need the glasses."

"That's what I figured," Gabriella said, "but I wanted to test it instead of guessing." She turned a page. "Here's my principle: check the pattern before you believe it. Two out of two friends fit it."

"Two friends is a small study," he said.

"I know. But it's a start."

Mikaela leaned over the counter. "She's going to survey the whole school now. I hope you know what you started."

"Sixth grade first," Gabriella said. She picked up the purple frames and set them on her nose, and the price tags on the wall behind the counter snapped into focus for the very first time. "These ones. Definitely these ones."

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move.
story:
The party had spilled from the kitchen into Mr. Ivanova's backyard, where the sandpit sat dry and arid after two weeks without rain, and someone had left a toy plane with a bent propeller nose-down in it. Lydia followed Nash and Cameron out there because the kitchen had gotten too loud, and because Mr. Ivanova had carried out his old wooden chess set and set it on the picnic table under the elm.

"You two play," Lydia said, and she settled onto the bench to watch.

The game went fine until move eleven. Cameron reached for her knight, lifted it, set it back on its square without moving it, and reached instead for her bishop. Nash slammed his palm on the table. "You can't do that. You picked it up. You have to move it."

"I put it back. It's like I never touched it."

"Takeback," Nash said, in the tone of someone accusing someone of a crime.

Lydia thought of the dispute she had watched at school last month, when two kids had shouted about a four-square line until the bell rang and nobody ever settled anything, and she thought that maybe this time it could go differently. She raised her voice just enough. "Hold on. Let's name the actual problem. The problem isn't whether Cameron is a cheater. The problem is we never agreed on a rule for touching pieces."

Cameron folded her arms. "There's no rule about touching."

"There is," Lydia said. "In real chess. It's called the touch-move rule." She had read it in a library book over the summer, and she was fairly sure she remembered it right. "If you deliberately touch one of your own pieces, you have to move it, if it has a legal move."

"That's not fair," Cameron said, but slower, like she was testing the words rather than throwing them.

"It's fair because it applies to both of you," Lydia said. "Nash touches a piece, Nash moves it. Same for you. One rule, both sides."

Nash looked at Cameron. Cameron looked at the knight, still sitting where she had left it, and then she picked it up again and moved it, losing her rook to Nash's bishop two turns later. She groaned, but she laughed too, and Lydia leaned back against the bench and watched the elm shadows slide across the board.

"Want the winner's seat next game?" Cameron asked her.

"Only if we say the touch-move rule out loud before anyone touches anything," Lydia said, and slid a black pawn toward her side of the board.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Nicholas had been chewing on the mystery all through lunch. Yesterday, in the group chat, Danica had written "Edith, why are you in the game store, you said you were broke" before Edith had mentioned any store at all. Edith had replied with a row of surprised faces and then gone quiet, which was not like her. So today Nicholas followed Danica into the computer lab after school and dropped his backpack on the table beside hers with a thump.

"You told the group chat exactly which store she was in," he said. "Nobody told you. I checked the messages twice."

Danica spun her chair around, looking pleased with herself. "It's called the Snap Map," she said, and pulled up the app on her phone. A map filled the screen, dotted with little cartoon faces. "It shows your real-time location to your friends, right on the map. It came out in 2017. Edith's bitmoji was standing in the game store at the mall. She never suspected a thing."

Nicholas leaned closer. His first idea was that the app just guessed, the way ads guessed, but a guess couldn't know a specific store at a specific minute. That meant the phone had to be telling the app where it was, constantly, whether Edith thought about it or not. He tested it the only way he could think of. "Walk to the water fountain," he told Danica. "I'll watch your face on my screen."

She marched off down the hall, and Nicholas watched her little cartoon self glide across the map at the same time, through the lab door, past the poster about the robotics club, stopping at the fountain. When she came back, he was grinning. "It works. It's like the app has a piston in it, pumping your location out every second, and you never feel it move."

"It's creepy if you think about it too long," Danica admitted. "I felt immune at first, like nobody would care where I was. Then a kid I barely know commented that I go to the bakery every Tuesday."

They found Edith in the library and showed her the screen, where her own face stood cheerfully in the school building, right next to theirs. Edith stared at it, then laughed, though her voice wobbled. "So that's how you knew about the game store. I was just looking, I didn't even buy anything." She found the settings and turned the sharing off, then exhaled like she'd set down something heavy. Nicholas noticed she kept her phone face down after that, even in the library, even though the map had gone dark.

At the door, Edith turned around. "Tuesday, bakery, me. Don't be weird about it."

"Too late," said Danica. "I'm already getting you a birthday cake shaped like a croissant."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: The urge to breathe is triggered mainly by rising carbon dioxide in the blood, not by falling oxygen.
story:
The basketball court behind the community centre had one cracked hoop and a chain-link fence, and through the fence Ethan could see the pool where his swim test would happen on Saturday. He missed a layup, then another, because he was watching the water instead of the rim. "You're playing like an eccentric scarecrow," said Ludovic, jogging over with the ball. "What's wrong with you?"

"I keep failing the twenty-five metres," Ethan said. "Front crawl, side breathing. I get halfway, feel like my chest is going to explode, and I grab the rope. Every single time." Ludovic spun the ball on one finger. "So breathe more," he said, which was exactly the kind of advice that sounded easy from someone standing on dry concrete. Ethan took a quick census of the pool through the fence: two lap swimmers, nobody in the slow lane. He had an idea, and he wanted to test it before Saturday, but he couldn't say yet what the idea was, because he wasn't sure it made sense.

He changed in the locker room, got in the slow lane, and pushed off. The first ten metres felt fine. Then the desperate feeling rose again, that panic like a hand squeezing his ribs. This time, instead of holding his air tight the way he always did, he let a slow stream of bubbles out through his nose, all the way until his face turned to breathe. The desperate feeling backed off. He reached the wall, gasping but there, twenty-five whole metres.

He hung on the gutter and worked it out, piece by piece. When he held air in, his body filled up with something that built and built until it screamed at him. When he let it out, the screaming came slower. "It's not air running out," he called to Ludovic through the fence, water dripping off his chin. "It's the built-up stuff I'm not letting go. The urge to breathe isn't about low oxygen, it's about that other thing rising." He climbed out, walked back through the gate, and picked up the ball. "Same game," he said. "First to eleven. I get the ball first."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Signposting words like 'first', 'second' and 'finally' tell listeners where they are in a speech, because they cannot flip back a page the way a reader can.
story:
Joshua stood at the front of his grandmother's kitchen with his note cards, ready for practice run number four. His speech was about why the school should invest in a garden, and he had a solid opening hook about a tomato that cost three dollars at the store. His grandmother settled onto a stool, folded her hands, and said she was all ears.

He made it through the hook and the first point, which was that gardens attract pollinators, when he noticed her forehead creasing. By the middle of his second point, about how vegetables you grow yourself are more nutritious than ones that sit in trucks for days, she raised a hand. "Wait," she said. "Which point is this? Are you still on the bees?"

He stopped. She had read his practice essay the night before and followed every line of it, so why was the same material falling apart in her ears? He glanced at his cards, and the difference jumped out at him. On paper she could flip back a page any time she got lost. Standing here, she only had his voice, moving forward, one direction, no going back. When he read his cards silently, he saw that he had buried his transitions inside long sentences where they vanished.

"Grandma, one more time," he said, and he flipped his cards over. In big letters he wrote FIRST, SECOND, FINALLY at the tops of three of them. He started over, and this time he said the words out loud, plain as road markers. When he said "second," her head nodded like something clicking into place, and she never lost the thread again. At school the next day he told Kaeden it was like discovering a whole ecosystem in the classroom, invisible systems keeping everything alive. Mr. Ivanova had overheard "first, second, finally" from the hallway and leaned in the doorway. "Signposting," he said. Joshua grinned and flipped to his clean copy. "Want to hear the run?"

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: A Scratch variable made 'for all sprites' can be used by every sprite, while one made 'for this sprite only' belongs to a single sprite.
story:
Eli dragged a "change score by 1" block into the coin sprite's script and clicked the green flag. The cat moved, the coins sparkled, the score stayed at zero. He clicked it again. Still zero. Mr. Nowak's computer lab rule said every project had to be tested twice before you asked for help, so Eli complied, running the whole game a third time while Blaine leaned over from the next seat.

"Vote for mine," Blaine said, holding out a shoebox with a slit cut in the lid. He was collecting ballots for whose game the class would demo at Friday's assembly, and he wanted to win. "You can't vote if your score doesn't even count."

"The score counts," Eli said. "Watch." He clicked the cat sprite's script, and the score went up, big and orange in the corner. Then he clicked the coin's script. Nothing.

Pierre spun his chair around from the far table. "Where'd you make the variable? In the cat?"

"So?"

"Make a new one," Pierre said. "Click the orange Variables, click 'Make a Variable,' and look at the choices." He went back to his own screen before Eli could ask anything else.

Eeli found the orange button. A box popped up with two options: "For all sprites" and "For this sprite only." His old score had the second one checked. He made a new score, picked "For all sprites," dragged his blocks over to it, and deleted the old variable. The green flag went up. The cat walked, the coin sparkled, and when Eli's arrow key sent the cat into the coin, the score jumped from zero to one. He grabbed a ballot from Blaine's shoebox, wrote his own name on it, and slid it through the slit.

"One to zero," Eli said. "The coin can finally keep score."

activity: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
knowledge_domain: to tune a violin or guitar by ear using a reference note
fact: A note one octave higher vibrates exactly twice as fast, so the A above A 440 vibrates 880 times a second.
story:
Lincoln held the guitar out at arm's length in the music room, as if it might bite him. Mr. Pereira had tuned all six strings before lunch, but somehow the low E string had gone flat, and the recital was in twenty minutes.

"Use the reference note," Mr. Pereira said, tapping the tuning fork on his knee and holding it near the high E string. It hummed, thin and bright, like a mosquito with good posture. "That string is your E. Match the low one to it."

"But they don't sound anything alike," Lincoln said. "One's like a bumblebee and one's like a foghorn." Tristen, who was tuning a violin nearby, snorted so hard he had to set his bow down. Isabelle patted Lincoln's shoulder without looking up from her sheet music.

Lincoln plucked the high E again and listened. Then he plucked the low string and turned the tuning key a tiny bit, the way Mr. Pereira had shown him, a quarter turn at a time, because cranking it was reckless and could snap the string. The two notes still refused to coincide. He tried singing the high note, then singing it lower and lower, sliding his voice down until it landed near the foghorn note. There was something odd in the way they rubbed together, a roughness that pulsed.

"Wait," he said slowly. "They have the same name. E and E. That's not a coincidence, is it?"

"Try humming both at once," Isabelle suggested. He did, and felt his own voice buzz against itself when the low note was close. He turned the key, plucked, hummed, turned again. When the rough pulsing flattened out into one smooth sound, Tristen raised his bow like a sword.

"That's it! Why does that work, though?"

"The low one vibrates half as fast," Lincoln said, grinning. "So my high E is doing exactly double the wobbles of his low E. Same note, different speed." He strummed a full chord and the whole guitar rang together, warm and round, filling the little room.

Mr. Pereira looked up from the piano. "Recital order just changed. You're opening, and I need someone to tune the others."

Lincoln picked up the tuning fork. "Whose guitar is first?"

activity: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
knowledge_domain: to explain the phases of the Moon by modelling it circling Earth with a lamp and a ball
fact: At full moon, Earth lies roughly between the Sun and the Moon, so we see the whole lit side.
story:
Lily's father handed her the tent bag and said the sleeping pad was the important part, because it would insulate her from the cold ground at night, and the ground was colder than most people guessed. Lily dragged it over to the fire circle, where Cruz was already waiting with the lantern from the picnic table.

"I get to hold the ball," Cruz said. "Mr. Menon said the person with clean hands gets the ball, and I washed mine twice." He turned the ball over, looking for a mark or a seam. "This is kind of trivial, right? Ball goes in a circle, done."

"It's not trivial if you can't explain why the shape changes," Lily said. Her want was simple: she had told Mr. Menon she could explain the Moon's phases at the campfire tonight, and she had never actually done it. He had loaned her the lantern and said, "Show me, don't tell me," which she was beginning to understand was harder.

She set the lantern on the cooler and made Cruz walk the ball in a slow circle around her, lamp sideways so it lit half the ball at every point. When the ball was near the lantern, she saw only a thin edge of light. When it moved to her side, half. Then Cruz stepped behind her, holding the ball out at arm's length behind her head, and his own shoulder cut off the light, leaving the ball in shadow.

"Your head is in the way," Lily said. "Move the ball higher."

"Then it's not level with the lamp."

"Higher, but keep the light reaching it. You can't block the lamp."

Cruz lifted the ball above her head, still behind her. The whole lit side faced her, a complete bright circle. "At full moon, Earth is between the Sun and the Moon," Lily said slowly, watching it. "So we see the whole lit side."

That evening, before the campfire talk, she found a folded note pinned under her flashlight: "I checked. It works. You owe me the first marshmallow. Cruz." Lily stuffed it in her pocket and held up the ball. "Okay. Cruz, stand behind me."

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: Solving 2x + 3 = 11 is the same as finding where the line y = 2x + 3 reaches a height of 11 on the graph, which happens at x = 4.
story:
Bentley had been stuck on problem seven for so long that the pencil had worn a flat spot. The community centre tutoring room smelled of old coffee and gym mats, and the clock above Ms. Popescu's desk ticked like it was being paid by the hour.

"Two x plus three equals eleven," Gwen read over his shoulder. "You just peel it. Minus three from both sides, then halve it. X equals four."

"That's what the algebra says," Bentley said. "But where is it? You write letters and numbers, and poof, an answer. I don't trust poof."

Gwen rolled her eyes, which was her way of agreeing to a challenge. She dragged a coordinate grid across the table, the kind with the tiny blue squares, and wrote y = 2x + 3 at the top. "Ms. Popescu says the equation has a line. Plot it and see for yourself."

So he did. He plugged in x = 0 and got y = 3, then x = 1 and got y = 5, then x = 2 and got y = 7. He plotted the points, and they fell into a straight line like they'd rehearsed it. Romane, who sat at the next table drawing what he called an eccentric dragon with sunglasses, leaned over. "Your dots are neater than my dragon."

"Everything is neater than your dragon," said Gwen.

Bentley devised a test, because he was tired of trusting things. If solving 2x + 3 = 11 meant finding x, and the line was built from the same numbers, then maybe the answer was hiding somewhere on the graph. He ran his finger up the y-axis to 11, then slid it sideways along the grid until it crossed the line. The crossing sat directly above the number 4 on the x-axis. He checked it twice. Then he did the algebra Gwen's way, peeling off the 3 and halving what was left, and got 4 again. Same answer, two different roads.

"Look," he said, turning the paper toward Gwen. "Where the line reaches a height of 11, that's x equals 4. That's what the equation was asking the whole time."

Gwen tried it herself with 2x + 3 = 13, hunting along her graph until she found where the line climbed to 13. "X equals 5," she announced, then did the algebra to check. "X equals 5. Huh."

Ms. Popescu wandered past their table, looked at the two grids, and said nothing, which for her was a standing ovation.

"There has to be a principle here," Bentley said, already copying a fresh problem onto a new sheet. "Every equation has a line somewhere, waiting to get caught."

Romane held up his dragon. "Everything has a graph if you're brave enough."

Bentley ran his finger up to 15 and started sliding sideways.

activity: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
knowledge_domain: to settle a disagreement over a game by naming the problem and agreeing on a fair rule
fact: In rock-paper-scissors, each choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one, so no choice is better than the others.
story:
Jasmine had been waiting all week for the water-balloon toss, and now the whole thing was stuck because Ibraheem refused to take turns fairly. He wanted rock every single time in rock-paper-scissors, and when Helen picked paper and beat him, he shouted that she had cheated.

"Rock always wins," Ibraheem insisted, holding up his fist like proof. "It's the strongest one. Everybody knows that."

Jasmine crouched in the grass by the picnic table and drew three quick shapes in the dirt with a stick: a rock, a pair of scissors, a sheet of paper. "Watch," she said. "Rock beats scissors. But scissors beats paper. And paper beats rock." She circled each shape with an arrow. "Every choice beats exactly one other choice and loses to exactly one. So no choice is better than the others. Rock is not the champion. It just beats scissors, and that's all."

Ibraheem squinted at the arrows. "Then how come I keep losing?"

"Because we both know what you'll throw," Helen said, grinning. "Your instinct is to pick rock every time. It's like telling everyone your move before you make it."

Mr. Haddad wandered over from the tranquil shade of the oak trees to see what the shouting was about, and Jasmine quickly explained the problem. "We can't decide who gets the first toss, and Ibraheem thinks rock is unbeatable." She stood up and brushed off her knees. "So here's my idea. We name the problem out loud, then agree on one fair rule. The problem is that Ibraheem always throws rock and then argues when he loses. The fair rule is: best two out of three, and nobody complains after, no matter what."

"Two out of three," Ibraheem repeated. He looked at the arrows in the dirt one more time, then at his own fist, and slowly uncurled it into flat paper. "Fine. But I'm mixing it up now."

They played right there on the spot. Ibraheem threw paper, Jasmine threw scissors, and Helen jumped up and down yelling, "See? Nothing is stronger than anything!"

"Round two," Ibraheem said, bouncing on his toes. "Watch closely, because this time I've got a whole new plan."

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: An ad hominem argument attacks the person making a claim instead of the claim itself, and it weakens a persuasive essay rather than strengthening it.
story:
Sophie sat at the kitchen table with her draft spread in front of her, a red circle glaring up from the middle of page two. Mr. Swampy had drawn it around the word lazy, which she had used to describe people who opposed the new weekend dog park at the pond. Her whole essay argued the park was a good idea, and calling the other side lazy had felt powerful, like a hammer. Now she wasn't so sure.

"What's the circle for?" asked Marius, who had come over to work on his own draft about school start times. He leaned across the table and read the sentence. "'Dog park opponents are just lazy people who don't want kids to have fun.' That's pretty fierce."

"It was my favorite line," Sophie said. "Why would he circle it if it's so strong?" She flipped to the back of her draft, where Mr. Swampy had written one word at the bottom: ad hominem. "I don't even know what that means."

Marius pulled out his phone, but Sophie stopped him. "Wait. Let me think first." She read her sentence again. Maybe the circle wasn't about grammar or word choice. Maybe it was about what the sentence actually did. Her sentence attacked the people, not their argument. That was the pattern she could see hiding under the red ink. "What if attacking the person makes the essay weaker instead of stronger?" she said slowly. "Because it doesn't answer anything they actually said?"

They tested it on her mom, who was impartial about the dog park and agreed to listen. Sophie read the lazy sentence, then swapped it for one that answered the neighbors' real complaint about noise. "Which one convinced you?" she asked.

"The second," her mom said. "The first one just made me wonder what you were hiding."

So the twist was that Sophie's weakest line had been her favorite, and her weakest material, the boring list of park rules about leashes and hours, might generate her strongest paragraph. She grabbed a pencil. "Marius, ask me the lazy question again," she said. "I want to hear what I say now."

Austin typed back, "How many people actually bought them?" Nobody answered that. Instead a new message appeared, a photo of a rapper named Dazzle holding the boosters over his head with the caption "Dazzle trusts HyperFlex. Do YOU?" Then Hargun's next message: "This is the greatest, most revolutionary shoe tech ever made. Haters will stay weak."

Austin put his phone down and stared at the ceiling. It was a weird feeling, like everyone was shouting the same three sentences from different accounts. He wrote in the chat: "Notice how nobody says what the shoe actually does? It's all 'everyone has it' and 'weak haters.'" Hargun replied, "Random hate, bro." Mackenzie sent a single message: "He has a point. My cousin bought them and they're just shoes." Then she went quiet, and the chat moved on to something else.

The next morning their class took the bus to the war museum. Mr. Tran led them past tanks and uniforms until they stopped at a wall of yellowed posters. One showed a crowd of faces with a slogan about standing together. Another used words like "parasites" and "traitors" in heavy black type. A third had a picture of a famous athlete shaking hands with a soldier.

"Read the plaque on the left," Mr. Tran said, and stepped aside.

Austin leaned in. In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. He said the name out loud, slowly. "Public Enlightenment and Propaganda. They had a whole ministry for this."

Hargun stood next to him, arms crossed. "So they made posters for a living?"

"They made posters to make everyone think the same thing," Austin said. "Look at this one. A crowd, so you feel left out if you disagree. That one uses gross words for people they didn't like." He pointed at the athlete poster. "And that one's like the Dazzle ad. Famous person, same trick."

Mackenzie crouched at the case, copying the plaque into her notebook. "Nineteen thirty-three," she said. "Before TV ads, even."

On the bus home, Austin opened the group chat. He typed: "The boosters aren't bad. The ads are just copying a museum wall." Then, before he could delete it, Mackenzie sent a photo of the crowd poster side by side with the HyperFlex ad. Hargun replied after a long minute: "Okay that's actually creepy."

An invasive pop-up covered half the screen, flashing FREE OFFER, and she had to hunt for the tiny x to close it. She sat back, arms crossed. That was not a science source. That was a billboard.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Nizar: "just search volcano. whatever's on top paid the most money to be there, that's how it works. my cousin told me."

Alexis stared at the screen. The top result did look like an ad, but the ones below it said things like "USGS Volcano Hazards Program" and "Smithsonian Global Volcanism." story:
Layla counted her birthday money in the food court: forty-three dollars, enough for the Starflash water bottle if she could find it cheaper than the price at the sports store. The billboard above the escalator showed the singer Zuri Mars holding the same bottle, gold letters spelling "Zuri trusts Starflash." Next to it, a poster claimed "Nine out of ten teens agree, Starflash is the bottle everyone wants." Her friend Oscar stood beside her, craning his neck at the poster.

"Or that's just what the sign wants you to think," Layla said. Avleen joined them carrying an orange smoothie, and Layla pointed at the poster. "They didn't say who the ten teens were. And just because Zuri Mars holds it, that doesn't mean she uses it. She got paid." She speculated that the store might put the same bottle on sale somewhere quieter in the mall, where there was no poster, because posters cost money and the price might cover it.

They found the bottle in a pharmacy near the east entrance, stacked in a plain cardboard display. The box said "Pure. Natural. Freedom in every sip." Layla turned it over and read the ingredient list on the wash label: it was a plastic bottle, made in a factory, with a hygiene sticker saying hand wash only. Nothing about the front matched anything on the back. "Glittering generalities," said Avleen, who had done a project on ads last year. "Vague, positive words like 'freedom' or 'natural.' They make you feel good without saying anything you can actually check." The pharmacy price was nineteen dollars, eleven less than the sports store.

Layla stood there turning the box in her hands. Maybe the words worked on her anyway, because the bottle still felt special, and that bothered her. She made herself a test: if she still wanted it without the box, she would buy it. She asked the cashier for one without a box, and the cashier dug one from under the counter, plain and identical. Layla looked at it for a long moment, then at Oscar, who was holding the blue box like it might vanish.

story:
Payton sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with the laptop propped on a stack of cookbooks, because the chair was too low and the screen otherwise showed her nothing but her own glare. Grandma's cat, a gray lump named Biscuit, slept on the windowsill where sun poured through the lace curtains and made warm stripes on the table. Payton had been building her first real game for two days: a little rocket that dodged falling stars. Her friend Jaxon had one at school that kept score, and Louane's had a countdown timer, but Payton's game did the worst thing a game could do. It counted nothing.

The problem was invisible. The rocket flew, the stars fell, and when a star touched the rocket, everything reset, but no number anywhere proved any of it had happened. She could not find a broken piece to fix, because nothing looked broken. So she made a guess: maybe a game that keeps score needs something called a variable, a labeled box that remembers a number. On Saturday, Jaxon came over with his own laptop, and she watched him click through his code. "See, mine's called score," he said, pointing at an orange block. "Change score by 1, every time you catch one."

That was the piece she had been missing. Payton went home and made a variable called score. When the green flag was clicked, she set it to 0, so every new game began empty. Then she dragged a "change score by 1" block into the star script, so each star the rocket dodged earned a point. She pressed the green flag, swooped under three stars, and the number in the corner climbed to 3. She exhaled, long and slow, like she'd been holding that breath all afternoon.

Grandma brought lemonade and watched over her shoulder. "Like a diplomat keeping a tally at a meeting," Grandma said, tapping the corner of the screen where the number sat. "Small points, one at a time, until the whole thing adds up." Payton grinned, because it was cumulative exactly like that: one, then two, then three, each point built on the last.

She still had to make the stars fall faster, and she hadn't figured out how to end the game yet. But when Jaxon texted "does it count now?", she sent him a photo of the screen showing score at 12, with Biscuit's tail draped across the keyboard.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by CBS director Tony Verna during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963.
story:
The whole living room smelled like popcorn, and Ethan had the best seat, the corner of the couch where he could see the TV and the door to the kitchen at the same time. His dad was in the armchair, Peyton sprawled on the rug, and Aniyah kept a running tally of every penalty on a napkin because she wanted to prove the refs favored the other team. Grandpa sat nearest the screen, leaning forward like the game might try to sneak past him.

Then the receiver bobbled the ball at the sideline, the official raised his arms, and the whole room erupted at once. "He was in!" Peyton shouted. "He was out by a mile," Aniyah said, waving her napkin. The announcer said the call was under review, and a moment later the play appeared again on the screen, frozen, then run in slow motion, the receiver's toe dragging a shower of chalk. Grandpa sat back and shook his head in wonder.

"You kids don't know how lucky you are," he said. "When I was your age, TV couldn't do that. If you missed a play, you missed it forever."

Ethan found that hard to picture. "Forever? What if the ref got it wrong?"

"Then you argued about it, and that was that," Grandpa said. "Nobody knew for sure."

Ethan chewed on that. How did the first replay even happen, and who decided to try it? He grabbed his mom's tablet from the side table, but Aniyah blocked it with her foot. "No spoilers," she said. "I'm budgeting my outrage for the fourth quarter." Peyton, meanwhile, had developed his own problem: the popcorn ran out ten minutes ago and he'd been drifting toward the kitchen ever since, too polite to say so. Ethan's dad finally tossed him the bag and said, "You handle the popcorn budget, I'll handle the remote."

On the tablet, Ethan found it, and he read it twice because it was better than he expected. "Grandpa, listen. Instant replay was first used in a live sports broadcast by a CBS director named Tony Verna, during the Army-Navy football game on December 7, 1963."

Grandpa was quiet a second. "Nineteen sixty-three. That's the year your grandma and I got married. So that whole fall, replays were brand new." Then he got an obstinate look, the same one he got about parallel parking. "I don't believe the picture could slow down back then. The machines weren't up to it."

"They were, for one play," Ethan said, "that's the whole point of it being first." He turned the screen so Grandpa could see for himself, and Grandpa squinted at it, and the ref on the big TV announced the call stood, and Aniyah groaned and crossed another mark on her napkin.

"They'd have called that wrong in your day," Ethan said.

"In my day," Grandpa said, "we'd still be arguing. And I'd be winning."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: In a fire, smoke and heat rise, so the cleaner, cooler air is near the floor, which is why firefighters teach people to crawl low under smoke.
story:
The bus smelled like hay and banana peels by the time it rolled through the farm gate. Madison pressed her forehead to the window and watched the orchard pass, its canopy of apple branches throwing cool shade over the pens below. Geese wandered between the fence posts, and her classmate Amirah pointed at a sign that read "Migrating geese keep out," which made Syed laugh, because the geese clearly could not read.

The teacher on the trip, Mr. Popescu, gathered everyone near the big red barn. Two firefighters were waiting there with a machine that puffed out harmless gray haze, the kind used for practice drills. "Today you learn what to do if smoke fills a room," one of them said. "Line up at the barn door. When the haze fills the entrance, you go through."

Madison stood in line and studied the doorway. The haze poured in and hung in the air, and she noticed something odd. The gray did not sink to the ground. It drifted upward and gathered along the ceiling, thick as wool, while the space near the dirt floor stayed almost clear. She crouched down to check, and from down there she could see clean air all the way under the fog. Smoke and heat rise, she thought, so the cleaner, cooler air must be near the floor. That had to be the trick.

Syed went first. He stood up straight and held his sleeve over his nose, then walked right into the haze and started coughing and waving his arms. He came out the other side blinking, with gray fluff in his hair. "I couldn't see anything," he said. "It was hot up there too."

"That's because you stood," Madison said. "Watch." She got on her hands and knees at the doorway and crawled forward, keeping her head low and her pace slow and consistent, the way she had decided a real crawl would need to be. She moved under the whole gray layer, and though the top of the haze churned like a storm cloud, the air she breathed felt cooler and clean. She reached the far side and stood up, dusty but grinning.

The firefighter knelt beside Syed, who had gone back for a second try. "That's why we teach crawling," he said. "Stay low under the smoke." Syed dropped to his hands and knees and made it through this time, and Amirah followed, laughing the whole way.

Afterward the class ate lunch under the apple trees, and the geese strutted past as if they planned to migrate somewhere better. Mr. Popescu handed out apples from the farm stand. Madison took a bite, then flopped back in the grass and looked up through the branches at the moving clouds. "Next time there's smoke," she said to Amirah, "I'm going under it."

story:
The pharmacy on Maple Street closed at six, and it was already ten to. Laurence stood by the shelf of cough drops while Anna-Eve counted her money for the third time, lips moving, coins trembling slightly in her cupped hands. Anna-Eve had been strange all week, and not in the fun, eccentric way she usually was, like the time she wore two different rain boots on purpose. This was different. She hadn't slept over on Friday. She'd stopped telling jokes. In science she'd pulled her sleeve down over her hands, and when the teacher called on her, her voice came out thin as paper.

"That's four ninety-two," the cashier said.

Anna-Eve stared at the coins like they were written in another language. "I have it," she whispered. "I just need to count again."

Laurence had an idea she wanted to test. She'd read the counselor's office poster so many times she could recite it: trusted adults a young person can tell about a worried friend include a parent, a teacher, a school counselor, the school nurse, or a doctor. The poster had bumblebees on it, sipping nectar from flowers, with a caption about how bees conserve their energy by resting between flowers. Laurence had thought that was a weird way to decorate advice, but it had stuck.

"You can get the honey-lemon ones," she said now, sliding her own two dollars onto the counter. "They taste like nectar, basically. My grandpa swears by them."

"That's not the point," Anna-Eve said, very quietly. "Everything feels loud lately. Even this store. Everything feels like it's about to fall on me."

Laurence put the cough drops in her backpack and took Anna-Eve's sleeve-covered hand. The cashier was pointing at the clock. Outside, the streetlights blinked on, and Laurence's mom was already idling at the curb, which gave them maybe ninety seconds.

"Monday morning," Laurence said, "before first bell, I'm walking with you to Ms. Wijaya's office. She's the counselor, and she has a jar of candy that's older than we are. You only have to say one true thing. I'll be right there."

Anna-Eve looked at the ground, then at the pharmacy doors, then back. "One true thing," she repeated.

"One," said Laurence, and pushed the door open into the cold blue evening, still holding on.

activity: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
knowledge_domain: to explain why the Roman Empire split and fell using a map of its borders
fact: To pay their armies during the crises of the 200s CE, Roman emperors put less and less silver into their coins, until some held only a few percent silver.
story:
Alexis unrolled the big laminated map across the archive table and weighted its corners with two reference books and an eraser. The Roman Empire at its largest looked like a fat horseshoe wrapped around the Mediterranean, and her assignment was to explain, out loud on Friday, why it split in two and then fell. She had a theory, but it felt shaky. "I keep drawing the borders," she told Charly, who had tagged along for her own reason. "But a map shows where the empire was, not why it broke."

Charly barely looked up. She was flipping through a box of catalogued photographs, hunting for one thing: her grandmother's shop, which had stood downtown sixty years ago. "Ms. Wanjiru said it might be in this collection," Charly said. "If it isn't, I don't know what I'll do for my presentation." Her voice wobbled on the last word.

Ms. Wanjiru set a small display case on the table beside the map. Inside lay two coins. The early one gleamed, bright and silvery. The later one was coppery and dull, almost orange. "The label is ambiguous," Alexis said slowly, reading it. "Silver content, varying. It doesn't say how much." She fetched the magnifying glass and squinted. The dull coin looked like it had started to decompose, the surface rough and greenish at the edges, nothing like the shining one. An assumption she hadn't known she was making, that Roman money stayed the same, cracked open in her head. Later, in a folder of translated documents, she found a message, a letter from a soldier in the 200s CE complaining that his pay arrived in coins that felt light and wrong. She cross-checked the archive's reference card and there it was: to pay their armies during the crises of the 200s CE, emperors had put less and less silver into their coins, until some held only a few percent silver. Armies, borders, the whole horseshoe. "That's it," she said. "They couldn't pay for the soldiers who held these borders, so the empire split in two to manage them, and then pieces fell off."

"Found it!" Charly shouted at the same moment, holding up a photograph of a tiny storefront with a striped awning. Then she paused. "Wait. Read the back."

On the photograph's reverse, in faded pencil, someone had written the date as both 1958 and 1963, with a question mark between them.

"So which is it?" Charly asked.

Ms. Wanjiru leaned over, tapping the map's western edge. "Some questions stay open in an archive," she said. "Yours, Alexis, has an answer. Charly's, maybe not."

Alexis rolled the map closed, coins and letter and crumbling borders all fitting together now, and Charly tucked the ambiguous photograph into her binder anyway. "I'll present it as a mystery," Charly said. "Maybe someone in the audience knows the right year."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
knowledge_domain: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
fact: In Canada, municipalities get their power to make bylaws from provincial laws, because the Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces control over municipal institutions.
story:
Tyler had decided that the school's bike racks were a disgrace. They leaned like tired old men, rusted and bent, and half the bolts had given up entirely. "Dilapidated," he announced at lunch, pointing through the window. "That's the official word. I looked it up."

"That's two official words," said Demi, "and zero bikes can park in them." Kamden slid his tray over and suggested they just fix the racks themselves with zip ties, but Tyler had bigger plans. Mr. Mehta had told the class that the racks were city property, and the city had a bylaw saying school grounds got new racks only every fifteen years. Fifteen! Tyler's bike would be a museum piece by then.

"So we petition the councillor," Tyler said. He'd learned the word that morning and liked the taste of it. Petition. It sounded like something you did while wearing a cape.

They spent two days collecting signatures, and then their count hit a plateau at thirty-seven and would not budge. Thirty-eight people had signed, but Kamden had signed twice, once as "Kamden" and once as "K. Denman, concerned citizen." So they enrolled Demi's little sister to work the Grade Four hallway, and the numbers climbed again. The real problem came later, when Tyler stood in front of Mr. Mehta's desk with the petition and a plan.

"Here's the thing," Tyler said. "The councillor will pass a new bylaw saying racks every five years instead of fifteen. Easy."

Mr. Mehta raised an eyebrow. "You might want to check who lets the city make bylaws in the first place. City Hall has a public info desk. Ask them."

Tyler took the bus downtown on Saturday with Demi, who came only because the info desk was next to a bakery. Behind the desk sat a woman with a stack of binders. Tyler asked his question, and she smiled like she'd been waiting all week for someone to ask it.

"Municipalities get their power to make bylaws from provincial laws," she said. "The Constitution Act, 1867 gives provinces control over municipal institutions."

Tyler stared at her. "So the city can't just pass anything it likes?"

"Not anything it likes."

"So my plan was like asking the janitor to redesign the whole school," Tyler said slowly, and Demi snorted so hard the bakery bag crinkled. But a petition was still a petition, and the woman showed him the form for asking council to reconsider a bylaw within the rules. Back at school on Monday, Kamden found him at lunch, marker already uncapped.

"New plan," Tyler said, flattening the form on the table. "Thirty-seven signatures. Make that two, because we're signing again, and this time you only get to be one concerned citizen."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
