fact: When ecologist Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave them ten minutes before Mr. Hosseini collected the lab sheets, and Alyssa still had a blank box where her food chain should go. Sun, grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. She had written that much, but the second question on the sheet asked what would happen if one link vanished, and she had no idea how to answer it.

"You could just guess," Gabryel whispered from the next stool. "He'll never know."

"He'll know," Alyssa said. She pulled the battered paperback Mr. Hosseini kept on the side counter, an old ecologist's memoir about studying the shore. She flipped pages, skimming for anything about Washington State. There it was, a chapter about a stretch of rocky shore where the writer had pried off every starfish, week after week, just to see what would happen. Starfish ate mussels, the page said. With the starfish gone, the mussels spread across the rocks until they crowded out many other species. One animal, eliminated, and the whole shore changed.

Alyssa read it twice. Then she tested the idea against her own chain. If the frogs disappeared, the grasshoppers would multiply the way the mussels had, and the snakes would go hungry and leave. It was the equivalent of pulling a single thread and watching the sweater unravel. She wrote it down: remove one link and the level below it takes over while the level above loses its food.

"Time," Mr. Hosseini called.

Alyssa handed her sheet in with her heart still pounding a little. At the end of class, he set it on her desk with a small check mark beside her answer.

"Read more of that memoir tonight," he said. "Chapter seven."

She grinned at Gabryel on the way out the door. "Told you he'd know."

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver.
story:
The morning of the debate tournament, Lea stood in the hallway outside Room 12 with her note cards fanned out like a poker hand. Her speech about school uniforms had an opening hook, three points, and a closing, exactly the way she had practiced. The trouble was the time limit. Two minutes. The buzzer would cut her off mid-sentence if she went long, and the judges were strict about that.

"Two minutes is nothing," said Bianca, pacing beside her. "You can't say anything important in two minutes."

Lea looked down at her cards. She had a hook about a girl sent home for wearing the wrong socks, three points with evidence, and a closing line she liked. On paper it filled four cards, and at her practice speed it ran closer to three minutes. Something had to go, but what? If she cut a point, her analysis felt thin. If she rushed, she would sound like she was reading a receipt.

She was still cutting when Bilal wandered over, munching a granola bar. "You know Abraham Lincoln gave a whole famous speech in about two minutes," he said. "The Gettysburg Address, November 19, 1863. It was only about 272 words."

Lea blinked. "Twenty-seven short of three hundred? That's it?"

"That's it," Bilal said. "People still memorize it."

So that was the hidden rule, Lea thought. It was not about filling time; it was about choosing words. She counted her cards and found she had written nearly six hundred. She crossed out every sentence that repeated an earlier one, kept her best evidence, and trimmed her closing to a single line.

When her turn came, she spoke without rushing. The buzzer stayed silent. Afterward, the judge held up her scoring sheet. "Nice structure," she said. "Hook, three points, close. And you actually landed the close."

Back in the hallway, Bianca was waiting. "Well?" she said. "How did you fit it all in?"

"I didn't," said Lea, grinning as she straightened her cards. "I left half of it out on purpose."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: Bulb filaments are made of tungsten because it has the highest melting point of any pure metal, about 3,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Annabelle spread her parts out on the picnic table beside the skate park: a battery, a bulb, a switch, and three wires with clips. Tomorrow Ms. Ngo would call on someone to build the circuit in front of the whole class and explain why the bulb lit, and Annabelle was determined that someone would be her.

Jaydon rolled up on his board, spraying gravel. "You're doing homework at a skate park?"

"Practice," Annabelle said. She clipped a wire to the battery, then to the bulb, then the third wire back through the switch. Nothing. She stared at it. The wires looked right, but looks could lie. Something invisible had to be missing, some path the electricity couldn't find. She unclipped the switch wire and touched it straight to the battery. The bulb glowed. So the problem was the switch, not the battery or the bulb. She opened the little plastic case and found a flap of metal bent away from its contact. She pressed it back and wired everything up again. Light.

"Whoa," said Jaydon, who had stopped mid-trick to watch. "How did you know it was the switch?"

"I didn't know. I tested it. If I skip the switch and it still doesn't light, the switch is innocent. If it lights, the switch is the criminal."

Louka wandered over, holding a museum postcard with a magnifier glued to it. "My grandpa says this thing cost half his pension, this museum membership, but look." Under the lens you could see a thin squiggle of wire inside a bulb. "Tungsten," Louka read off the back. "It has the highest melting point of any pure metal. About 3,400 degrees Celsius."

"That's what's in my bulb? That skinny little squiggle?" Annabelle held the card up beside her glowing bulb. The same zigzag, glowing hot enough to shine without melting. She had been ready to guess the glass did the shining, or the battery somehow pushed light through the wire. Now she knew better.

Jaydon checked the sun sliding behind the fence. "You've got ten minutes of daylight left, then I'm reclaiming this table for skate stuff."

"Deal," Annabelle said, and pulled out a second bulb. "Louka, hold the wires while I time myself. Sixty seconds, starting now."

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: If the user types a word such as 'seven', Python's int() raises a ValueError, and the program stops unless the error is handled.
story:
The basement smelled like popcorn and old carpet, and Jordan's fingers hovered over Deacon's keyboard. On the screen glowed five lines he had typed himself: ask for a number, then loop ten times and print each line of the times table. He had been working on it since Tuesday, when his grandmother had leaned over his shoulder at home and said, "Make me one, sweetheart. I never learned my sevens." He could still picture her copying his first attempt onto a napkin, next to her coffee cup, promising she would try it that very night.

"Run it," said Deacon, bouncing a tennis ball off the ceiling pipes. Ares leaned in from the beanbag chair, chewing a pretzel.

Jordan typed 7 at the prompt. Ten lines rolled out, 7 times 1 equals 7, all the way to 7 times 10 equals 70. Ares pumped his fist. "It works!"

So that evening, Jordan set his grandmother in front of the laptop at home. She typed, carefully, with one finger: seven.

The screen turned red with error text. ValueError, it said, and a word he didn't recognize, int(). The program had just stopped, and his grandmother looked like she'd broken something. "Oh, honey, I'm sorry. Did I ruin it?"

He told her no, and all night he puzzled over it. The pattern was clear when he lined up the two tries: 7 had worked, seven had not. The program tried to transform whatever the user typed into a whole number, and a word wouldn't go. That was the hidden rule, invisible until you bumped into it.

Back in Deacon's basement on Saturday, he tested the idea. He typed seven at his own prompt, watched the same red error appear, then typed a few new lines around the loop, and typed seven again. This time a small message printed instead: Please type a number, like 7. The program kept going.

"Is that a factor of it?" Ares asked, squinting at the screen.

"No, that's the loop," Jordan said. "The loop does the multiplying. The new part just catches the mistake so the whole thing doesn't quit." He thought of his grandmother's one careful finger on the keys. "Nobody should feel like they broke it just because they typed a word."

He emailed her the new version, and Sunday morning a reply arrived: it worked, she wrote, all the way up to 7 times 12 equals 84.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
knowledge_domain: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
fact: Many persuasive essays end with a call to action, a sentence telling the reader exactly what they should do next.
story:
The clock on Grandma's mantel ticked toward four, and Charlotte had until dinner to finish her essay about Riverside Park. Grandpa had let her spread her papers across his kitchen table, which smelled of coffee and the lemon polish he used every Saturday. Her three middle paragraphs were solid: the park's rusty swings, its cracked basketball court, the trash nobody collected. But her ending kept stopping after "so the park matters to a lot of people."

She remembered the afternoon she had lost the school essay contest last spring. Her piece about the cafeteria menu had been careful and organized, and she had still come second to a boy whose final line asked everyone to fill out the survey in the office. At the time she thought the judges had simply liked his handwriting better. Now, on Grandpa's porch after lunch, she had asked him what he thought, and he had shrugged. "Sounds like he ended with a call to action," Grandpa said, peeling an orange. "A sentence telling the reader exactly what they should do next."

Charlotte turned that over while she sharpened her pencil, listening to the blades grind. It was like a hidden rule nobody had written down. Her essay had ended; his had pushed. She decided to test the idea right here. She flipped to a clean page and wrote a new ending: "Sign the petition at the hardware store on Miller Street this weekend." Then she read both versions aloud to Grandpa, one after the other.

The first ending dropped into the quiet kitchen and stopped, like a stone in still water. The second one made Grandpa set down his orange and reach for his coat. "When does the hardware store close?" he asked. Charlotte grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. She copied the new ending into her final draft, her pen racing the mantel clock, and then slid the pages into her backpack and ran for the door, calling over her shoulder, "Five o'clock, Grandpa. We can make it by five."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Lucy laced her skates in the cold hallway of the rink and watched Aubree wince as she sat down. Aubree had been brilliant at yesterday's first day of tryouts, fastest in every drill, and she had skipped out grinning. Now she gripped the bench and lowered herself like her legs were made of glass.

"I felt amazing last night," Aubree said. "This morning I could barely climb my stairs. My mom thinks I hurt something, but I don't remember falling."

Lucy thought about that. If Aubree had actually pulled a muscle, it would have hurt right away, on the ice, where it happened. Instead she'd felt nothing until today, a whole day later. That meant the soreness probably wasn't an injury at all. She remembered her cousin complaining the same way after her first hockey camp, fine that evening and stiff as a board the morning after. Lucy had looked it up then, and now the memory clicked into place.

"It's delayed onset muscle soreness," Lucy said. "Soreness from a workout you're not used to shows up a day to three days later, not right away."

"So it's normal?" Aubree asked.

"It's normal. It just has terrible timing." Lucy held out a hand and pulled her up. "But it doesn't have to intimidate you out there. Those eighth graders look like a predatory wall of muscle, but half of them are probably going to be limping tomorrow, since this is hard for them too."

Aubree laughed for the first time that morning. Kareem, tying his skates beside them, leaned over. "Wait, that's a thing? Because I was planning to hide in the locker room with a fake stomachache."

"Don't you dare," Aubree said. "You've wanted the wing spot since fourth grade."

When Mr. Okonkwo called them onto the ice, Aubree took the first lap slow, testing her legs like she was checking ice thickness. By the third lap she was low and fast again. Lucy passed her once and saw her grin.

The tryout list went up at noon. Aubree found her name, then Kareem's, then grabbed Lucy's sleeve and pointed three lines down.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Pencils marked H have more clay and make lighter, harder marks, while pencils marked B have more graphite and make softer, darker marks.
story:
Henry had been coming to the community art studio every Saturday for a month, and today Mr. Gill had set a single white ball on the table under a lamp. "Spheres," Mr. Gill announced, clapping his hands like a game show host. "If you can make a flat circle look round, you can draw almost anything."

Morgan, who sat next to Henry and drew horses on every surface she owned, got stuck immediately. She scribbled and scribbled at the shadowed side of her sphere, but it stayed pale and stubborn. "My shadow looks like the ghost of a shadow," she groaned, holding up her pencil and squinting at it. "There are letters on these things. A 2H. That means something, right? Like a secret code?"

Henry leaned over. He looked at Morgan's pale sphere, then at his own, then at the cup of loose pencils in the middle of the table. His shadow wasn't dark enough either. He picked up a 2H and a 4B and made two quick swipes on the corner of his paper. The H line came out light and crisp. The B line came out soft and black as a shoe. He tried a 6H, and it barely left a mark at all, like the pencil was shy. That was a pattern, and patterns meant something. He tested one more pair just to be sure the first wasn't a fluke, and it wasn't. The more H, the lighter; the more B, the darker.

"Okay, I think I've got it," he said, arranging the pencils in a line across the table like suspects in a lineup. "The H ones and the B ones are opposites." He pointed at the Hs. "These are the light, hard ones." Then the Bs. "These are the soft, dark ones. So your 2H can't make a real shadow because it's just built to be light." Morgan frowned at her ghostly sphere, then at the 6B Henry handed her.

"You mean I've been fighting my own pencil this whole time?" She pressed the 6B down on the shadow side and her eyes went wide. The darkness bloomed under her thumb, deep and real, and a cast shadow spread out from the bottom of the sphere, away from the lamp. "It's alive," she whispered. "It's spreading like a virus." Mr. Gill, passing behind them, said the only thing wrong with that was that it was catching, and indeed Henry had already grabbed a 4B to darken his own sphere's shadow.

By the end of the session, both spheres looked round enough to roll off the page. Mr. Gill walked around the table and paused at Henry's drawing for a significant moment, long enough that Henry held his breath. "Well," Mr. Gill said, "I was going to teach the pencil thing next week, but you two seem to have contradicted my lesson plan." Morgan grinned and slid her drawing across the table. "Next Saturday, can we find out what the F stands for?"

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: In Python, range(1, 11) produces the numbers 1 to 10, stopping just before its second number, so a table up to 12 needs range(1, 13).
story:
Alex had promised Harlow a times-table program by the end of lunch, and the clock on the wall of the computer lab said he had nine minutes.

He typed the number 7 at the prompt, hit Enter, and the screen printed 7, 14, 21, 28, all the way down in neat rows. He leaned back, feeling buoyant, until he counted the lines. Eleven. His loop said range(1, 12), and somewhere in there the machine had decided a times table meant seven ones through seven elevens, which was a bold opinion.

Yesterday Ms. Bautista had written range(1, 11) on the board and told them it gave 1 to 10. Alex remembered because he had assumed it gave 1 to 11, raised his hand, and been wrong in front of everyone, which still made his ears warm when he thought about it. He ran a quick test now: for i in range(1, 11): print(i). The numbers climbed to 10 and stopped. So the second number was where the machine quit, not what it reached. Range stopped just before it. That was the rule, and the rule had quietly eaten his twelfth line.

"What's wrong?" Harlow asked, sliding into the next chair.

"It stops at eleven. Nobody wants elevens. My grandma quizzed me on twelves at every dinner. That's probably why."

Harlow squinted at the screen. "So make it go higher."

"I'm not raising it, I'm aiming past the number I want. Like throwing to the cutoff man." He changed the 12 to a 13 and ran it again. Twelve rows marched down the screen, ending at 84, bold as anything.

Harlow read them aloud in a whisper, all the way to twelve twelves.

"Type in your worst number," Alex said, and Harlow's finger was already reaching for the 8.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: A null hypothesis is the statement that there is no relationship between the things being studied, which an experiment then tries to reject.
story:
Megan stood behind her table at the science fair and stared at her two bean plants, the one that had been listening to Mozart all week and the one that had sat in silence. The silence plant was taller. Her display board said "Music Helps Plants Grow," and now it looked like a lie.

Harmony leaned over from the next table. "Yours lost?"

"Mine got weird," Megan said. She had measured both plants every day, and the quiet one had grown two centimeters more. Guneet crouched down to look at her data chart, where the two lines crossed halfway through the week.

"You need to say what 'no effect' would look like," Guneet said, pointing at her empty results section. "Ms. Park kept writing that on my draft."

Megan frowned. "What do you mean?"

"Like, before you start, you write down the boring answer. The one where the music does nothing." He tapped her chart. "If the plants grow about the same, that's it. My brother says it's called the null hypothesis."

"The null hypothesis," Megan repeated, writing it at the top of a fresh card. She read it aloud as she printed: "There is no relationship between music and plant growth." Then she drew an arrow to her crossed lines. The growth amounts were almost the same, only a few millimeters apart, close enough that they could signify nothing at all. Her experiment hadn't proved music helped. It had come pretty close to proving the boring answer, or at least failing to knock it down.

Ms. Park stopped at the table and looked for a long moment. "What happened here?"

"I tested a guess and it didn't hold up," Megan said. "The quiet plant did fine. It was kind of resilient, actually. I want to try again with ten plants and a control, even if it means the expense of another packet of seeds."

Ms. Park smiled. "That's the sentence I wait all year to hear."

Megan turned her board around, crossed out the old title, and wrote: "Round Two."

activity: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
knowledge_domain: to put a bandage on a cut and know when a wound needs a doctor
fact: An animal bite that breaks the skin should be checked by a doctor, because bites can carry germs deep into the wound.
story:
Bentley had been nominated as first-aid monitor for Ms. Barrett's class field trip to the bank, which mostly meant he carried the little red kit and hoped nobody needed it. He had spent all week practicing at home with a roll of gauze and his little sister's cartoon bandages, learning to press a clean pad over a cut, hold it firm, and wrap the bandage without making it so tight the fingers turned purple. His dad, who ran the pharmacy on Miller Street, had quizzed him every dinner. "Good bandage," he'd said last night. "Tomorrow I'll show you when a cut needs a doctor."

At the bank, a man was waiting in line with a small brown dog on a leash, sitting politely beside his shoes. While Ms. Barrett talked to the teller about the class tour, Jett crouched down and wiggled his fingers near the dog's face. Bentley saw the whole thing: the dog startled, snapped, and Jett yanked back his hand with a yelp.

"It barely got me," Jett said, but two red dots were beading on his knuckle. Bentley's stomach did a flip, but he made himself think. He led Jett to the bench by the deposit slips, washed the spot with a wipe, and pressed a clean pad on it, exactly the way he'd practiced. Small scrape, bandage, done. But this was a bite, and the skin was broken. Something his dad had said came back to him, and though doubts plagued him, he kept turning it over. A bite was different from a scrape. It could push germs in deep, where a bandage couldn't reach.

"Ms. Barrett," he said, holding up Jett's wrapped hand, "it's a bite, and it broke the skin. I think he needs a doctor."

She looked at the knuckle, then at the dog's owner, who had already stepped out of line. "You're right, Bentley. That's exactly the call to make." She turned to Jett. "We'll call your mom from the office."

Jett sighed, but he flexed his fingers and managed half a grin. "Guess you finally got to use the kit."

"Guess I did," Bentley said, snapping the red case shut.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Since Canada stopped distributing pennies in 2013, cash totals there are rounded to the nearest five cents, while card payments are still charged to the exact cent.
story:
Alexis stood outside the corner store with a five-dollar bill in her fist and her mother's voice in her head: one carton of milk, walk straight there, count your change. Andrea had come along to supervise, which mostly meant eating chips on the bench out front.

"Watch me be competent," Alexis announced, and pushed through the door. The checkout machine emitted a cheerful beep as she set the milk on the belt. The screen showed 3.02.

She handed over the five. The cashier gave her back two coins, a toonie and a nickel. Alexis stared at the nickel. Two dollars she understood, but five cents meant she'd paid 3.00, not 3.02.

"Excuse me," she said, "you gave me an extra two cents." She held out the nickel like evidence, feeling helpful and slightly heroic.

The cashier smiled. "Cash totals get rounded to the nearest five cents. Card payments are still charged to the exact cent. You paid cash, so 3.02 became 3.00."

Alexis walked out slowly, turning this over. Rounding. Card, exact. Cash, rounded. She plopped down beside Andrea. "The register didn't make a mistake. There's a rule, an invisible rule, and I met it."

"And you tried to return money," Andrea said. "You tried to give money back to a store. That's like a parasite apologizing for biting."

"I was being honest!"

"You were being a menace to the economy."

Alexis ignored her. She wanted proof, not just one cashier's word. Andrea had bought a juice earlier with her card; Alexis made her check the receipt. There it was, charged to the exact cent, no rounding at all. One cash total rounded, one card total exact, two experiments, one pattern. Science.

Then came the twist. Alexis counted her money again and realized the rounding had been secretly working in her favor the whole time, like a tiny invisible ally. Two cents free. She marched back in and set two pennies from her pocket on the counter.

"Rounding refund," she declared.

"We don't take those anymore," the cashier said gently.

Alexis picked up her pennies, feeling her cheeks go warm. Back on the bench, she and Andrea divided the nickel she'd "saved," and Alexis put the pennies in the gumball machine, which ate them and emitted nothing at all.

"Even the machine rounds," said Andrea.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
Marcus had one job this morning: welcome the new exchange student before first period. Ms. Hassan had said it twice, once at the door and once in the hallway, as if she suspected he might forget.

The new kid was already at his locker, a small boy in a gray jacket, arranging his shoes with the care of someone setting up a chess board. When he turned and saw Marcus, he bowed. It was quick and shallow, like a nod that had gotten away from him. Marcus stuck out his hand. The boy looked at it, then shook it, very politely, as if the hand were a package he had to sign for. Behind Marcus, Lenny whispered, "Ten bucks says he does that all day." Marcus didn't take the bet. Lenny's bets thrived on other people being wrong.

At lunch, things got more interesting. The boy's grandmother had packed him noodles, and he ate them with a slurping so loud that Alia, three seats down, stopped chewing. "In his house that probably means the food's good," she said. Lenny pointed out that in Marcus's house it meant you got sent to the porch. At Alia's table, her grandmother insisted you left a little food on the plate to show you were full; at Marcus's, leaving food meant you'd hurt the cook's feelings. The same noodle, three different rules. Marcus filed this away.

The bowing, though, was the part he couldn't stop watching. When Ms. Hassan returned the boy's dropped pencil, the boy bowed deep and slow, holding it, so low his face nearly met his binder. When Lenny tossed him a milk carton, he bowed short and quick again. Same kid. Different bows. Marcus ran the two moments in parallel, side by side, and the pattern showed up like a watermark: deeper and longer meant more respect. Ms. Hassan, teacher, pencil returned, deep bow. Lenny, milk carton, flick of a bow. No offense to Lenny.

So Marcus tested it. On his way out, he stopped, faced the boy, and bowed low and slow, counting silently to three. When he straightened up, the boy's whole face had changed, like sun coming through a window. He bowed back just as deep, and then held out something wrapped in wax paper, two rice crackers from his lunch. A gift, apparently, for a proper greeting. Lenny, watching from the water fountain, bowed too, quick and shallow, just to see. The boy smiled and gave him nothing.

"Depth matters," Marcus said, and ate his cracker all the way to the bus line.

activity: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
knowledge_domain: to compare a plant cell and an animal cell and name the parts only plants have
fact: Plant cells have a stiff cell wall outside the cell membrane, made mostly of cellulose, which animal cells do not have.
story:
Asher had begged for this Saturday shift at the clinic ever since his cat was patched up here in March, and today Mr. Horváth finally handed him a real job: hold the rabbit, Dolley, still while the vet checked her sore paw. In the waiting room, Asher's friend Mael sat with his hamster's empty travel cage on his lap. "She died Tuesday," Mael said. "I brought the cage to return the bedding they gave us."

"Then you're on the jury with me," Asher said, pointing at the two lunch bags on the counter. He had brought celery and ham, because Mr. Horváth had promised to settle a debate. "Mael says celery crunches because it's fresher than meat. I say it's something else."

Mr. Horváth washed his hands, snapped the rabbit's check finished, and waved them over. "Show me." Asher bit the celery stalk; it cracked like a twig. Then he bent the slice of ham, which folded and folded without breaking. "See, they're both made of cells," Asher said, "but the celery keeps winning."

Mr. Horváth pulled an old chart from a drawer and let them hold it. Asher traced the little rectangle drawn around each plant cell. "Cell wall," he read aloud. "Outside the membrane. Made mostly of cellulose." He looked up fast. "And animal cells don't have one at all?" The vet only smiled and pointed at Dolley, nibbling in her carrier, skin flexing smooth as she moved.

"So it's not freshness," Asher said. "It's armor. Every celery cell is boxed in stiff stuff, and ham cells aren't boxed in anything." Mael turned the ham slice over twice, then set it down and picked up the celery. "I change my mind," he said. "Fresh was a bad guess." Asher laughed and took a victory bite so loud the rabbit's ears shot straight up. He was going to nurture this idea all the way to Monday's science class, where it would make his textbook diagram look practically obsolete. "Watch," he told Mael, and snapped one more stalk in half.

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: An answer like six eighths should be simplified by dividing the top and bottom by their greatest common factor, 2, to get three quarters.
story:
At the tutoring centre, Isabelle kept one eye on the folder Ms. Mwangi was carrying. Inside it was last week's fractions quiz, and Isabelle wanted hers back before the other kids arrived. Her mother had promised extra screen time for every perfect score, and this week she was sure she had earned one. She had added one half and one eighth by finding a common denominator of eight, changed one half to four eighths, and written her answer as six eighths. It had felt like the best work she had done all term.

Ms. Mwangi set the folder on the front desk and went to help a boy with a worksheet. Isabelle crept forward, but Lane got there first, flipping through the stack. "You got mine already?" he asked, pulling out his page and then hers. He held hers up so she could see the red checkmark at the top, and Isabelle's heart jumped. A checkmark meant full marks.

Then she saw the small red circle around her answer, and beside it one word: unfinished.

"That's a check," Lane said. "It counts."

"It doesn't look like it counts," Isabelle said. She took the page and stared at six eighths until the numbers blurred. The answer was right. She had checked it twice. Unless the answer was right and still wrong somehow, like a pattern hiding underneath the numbers. She thought of birds that migrate south even when the weather is still warm, following a rule you can't see. Maybe fractions had an invisible rule too. She grabbed her pencil. Six and eight were both even, so she tried dividing the top and the bottom by their greatest common factor, 2, and got three quarters.

She carried the page to the desk. "Is this what it wanted?"

Ms. Mwangi looked at three quarters and nodded. "Now it's finished."

Allyson, who had just come in and dropped her bag beside Isabelle's, leaned over the page. "Wait," Allyson said slowly, "that's my handwriting." She pulled the same quiz from her own binder, with the same red circle. Isabelle looked again. The paper in her hand had Allyson's name in the corner, smudged, and the stack had been shuffled. Her own quiz was still in the folder.

Isabelle went back, hands shaking, and found hers. She had forgotten to simplify six eighths too. "Get me that pencil," she said.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Phone batteries are lithium-ion, and as they chemically age they hold less charge, so battery life slowly gets shorter.
story:
Gabriella pressed her nose against the display case while the smell of lemon polish and new plastic filled the air. Behind the glass, rows of phones gleamed under bright lights. Her old phone, which had been her cousin's before it was hers, sat heavy in her pocket, dead again, even though she had charged it all night. At school it never lasted past lunch, and today she planned to find out why.

Gael met her at the counter, swinging his backpack. "Mine died during the math quiz," he said, pulling out his own hand-me-down with its cracked corner. "Every single day."

The shop assistant, Ms. Siddiqui, slid a small card across the counter. It showed a battery shape with the words "lithium-ion" printed underneath. Gabriella picked it up and turned it over, thinking hard. Her cousin had used that phone for three years before passing it down, and Gael's brother had used his even longer. The brand-new phones in the case had never belonged to anyone.

"Wait," Gabriella said slowly. "The batteries are lithium-ion. As they chemically age they hold less charge, so the battery life slowly gets shorter." She looked at Gael. "Ours are old. That's why they die by lunchtime. It's not because we're doing something wrong."

Gael's face went from defiant to relieved, like he'd been blaming himself all along. "So a new battery would fix it?" he asked Ms. Siddiqui.

She checked his model and shook her head. "For that one, a replacement battery costs almost as much as this." She tapped a basic phone in the case, the one Gabriella's mother had agreed to pay for if Gabriella covered half from her savings. "This one holds a charge all day."

Gabriella counted her money on the counter, crumpled bills and coins that smelled like her pencil case. There was also a flyer beside the register: the store would let kids enroll in a free workshop on using phones safely, and one student each month became a student ambassador, helping others learn.

"Gabriella, look," Gael whispered, pointing at the flyer. "You'd be good at that."

She smoothed her last coin onto the pile and smiled at Ms. Siddiqui. "Sign me up for both," she said. "The phone and the workshop."

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: A blending stump, or tortillon, is a tightly rolled paper stick used to smooth pencil shading into gradual tones without using your finger.
story:
Edouard sat at the kitchen table with a pencil, an orange, and a lamp he had dragged in from the living room. Ms. Russo had shown the class a drawing of a sphere in art yesterday, and next week each of them had to hand in their own, with a highlight, a shadow, and a cast shadow. His first attempt looked like a flat grey circle with a smudge on one side. He stared at the orange under the lamp and wondered where the light actually went, since it seemed to slide around the curve instead of stopping anywhere.

His classmate Ines had posted her sphere online last night, and the comments said it looked like mud because she had rubbed it with her finger. Edouard remembered her complaining at lunch that her paper had gone shiny and greasy in the smudged spots. He rubbed his own thumb along the shading he had done, and sure enough, the graphite smeared into a blotch with a faint sheen. So that was the pattern: fingers left marks, pencils left lines, and neither one made the smooth, gradual tones in Ms. Russo's example. Something had to exist that did.

He texted Charles-Olivier, who had an older cousin in art school. Charles-Olivier sent back a photograph of a thin paper stick, pointed at one end, tightly rolled from a small sheet of paper. "It's called a tortillon," he typed, "or a blending stump. You use it instead of your finger." That evening Charles-Olivier commuted over on his bike with two of them in his backpack, and Edouard took one and tried it on a corner of his drawing.

The paper tip picked up graphite and glided it around in tiny circles, and the harsh band of shadow softened into the lit side so gradually that he could not say where one ended and the other began. No shine, no blotch. Edouard leaned close to the orange, noticing how the darkest shadow sat opposite the lamp and the cast shadow stretched away from the light in a long ellipse. He wondered whether the shadow would shift if he moved the lamp, so he slid it an inch to the left and watched the whole pattern swing on the curved skin like a slow door.

He worked until the kitchen went dim, keeping his wrist agile with quick light strokes, and the sphere on his page began to look round instead of flat. Then he set down the tortillon, picked up the orange, and took a bite.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats.
story:
Alexander carried the wiggling puppy in his arms the whole way to Maple Park, because today was the first day of his whole entire life with a dog. Biscuit was small and brown and his ears flapped like little flags when the wind caught them. Alexander had promised his mom he would walk him, feed him, and learn everything about him, and he had already read fourteen pages of a puppy book before breakfast.

At the water fountain he found Arnaud and London tossing a Frisbee. "You got the dog?" Arnaud shouted, sprinting over. "He's real! He's actually real!" Biscuit squirmed down into the grass, bounced in a circle, then chased his own tail twice. London dug into her backpack and pulled out a bag of trail mix. "Dogs love treats," she said, crouching down and shaking the bag so Biscuit came running. She held out a handful with peanuts, chocolate chips, and raisins right in the middle.

"Wait!" Alexander grabbed her wrist before Biscuit's nose reached it. He had read those fourteen pages, and one paragraph had jumped out at him so hard he'd read it twice. "Grapes and raisins can cause kidney damage in dogs, so they should never be given as treats." He said it fast, like a fire alarm. Arnaud looked at the raisins, then at Biscuit, then at the raisins again. "Kidney damage," he repeated slowly, and pulled the bag away.

London sat back on her heels. "My uncle had a dog, Muttsy, who got really sick once," she said. "Nobody ever knew why. He was so buoyant one day, bouncing around, and the next he was at the vet for a week." She frowned at the trail mix. "He used to eat whatever we dropped at cookouts. Picnic food." Alexander's mind buzzed. A dog who ate dropped picnic food, and got mysteriously sick, and grapes and raisins are picnic food. He couldn't prove it, but the pattern made his arms prickle. "That's more than an anecdote," he said. "That's evidence."

"Okay, no trail mix for Biscuit," London said, sealing the bag. Then came the twist. Arnaud pulled out his phone to look up what dogs could eat, and scrolled with his eyebrows going higher and higher. "Guys," he said. "Chocolate's bad for them too." All three of them stared at the chocolate chips still sitting in the bag.

"Puppy book," Alexander announced, holding up his hand. "Chapter five. I'm way ahead of you." Biscuit barked once, loud and certain, and stole the Frisbee clean out of the grass. "Hey!" Alexander laughed, and raced after him across the park.
